A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LaTo system and HFL-150K dataset. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original face-editing comparisons, component ablations, landmark-predictor evaluations, dataset-scaling experiments, and human validation of the rectified identity metric.

after.justification: v2 retains these results and adds a direct editing-quality user study, codebook ablations, robustness examples, demographic analysis, and qualitative facial-animation results.

M1.justification: The original image-editing method remains unchanged, but v2 Appendix C.3 introduces a substantive video adaptation: a 3D tokenizer spanning 81 frames, a Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone, and an additional cross-attention layer trained while the original backbone weights remain frozen. This extends the procedure to reference-video-driven facial animation.

E1.justification: v2 adds facial animation using a 16K OpenHumanVid-derived corpus with landmark trajectories and captions, extending beyond the original image-editing tasks. Section 4.3 also adds incomplete-landmark and ambiguous-instruction scenarios. The original benchmarks remain; Appendix B.3's demographic statistics describe existing HFL-150K data rather than a newly sampled population.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained editing, landmark-prediction, and captioning experiments is unchanged. The new human-rating study evaluates the already benchmarked Step1X-Edit† and FLUX.1-Kontext† under an additional evaluation protocol. Wan2.2 is the video adaptation's backbone, not an evaluated competing baseline.

E3.justification: The original splits, training settings, and metrics remain unchanged. Added experiments introduce a five-point human-rating protocol covering 1,110 cases with 21 valid participant responses, landmark masking at 10%, 30%, and 50%, and codebook reconstruction evaluation using L1 distance and PSNR on rendered landmarks. The video experiment also introduces an 81-frame training configuration.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of quantization necessity and codebook capacity through a no-quantization variant and three codebook sizes (Table 9). It adds incomplete-landmark and ambiguous-instruction robustness tests, further cross-identity and stylistic examples, and demographic composition analysis. The existing positional-encoding, CFG, unconditional-token, and data-scaling analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or a specified significance-testing procedure for the benchmark gains. v2's new tables likewise report aggregate values without uncertainty. The code-vector similarity mean and standard deviation in Appendix D.1 are unchanged; the new participant count concerns study sample size.

E6.justification: Tables 1–7 retain their values. New Table 8 reports overall human ratings of 0.811 for LaTo, 0.770 for FLUX.1-Kontext†, and 0.761 for Step1X-Edit†. Table 9 reports L1/PSNR of 3.67/21.33 for 8,192 codes versus 7.04/19.11 without quantization. Demographic estimates and qualitative robustness, ambiguous-instruction, and video-animation findings substantially expand the reported evidence.

T1.justification: Equations 1–8, including the tokenizer objective, positional encoding, rectified identity score, and filtering definition, are retained. Algorithm 1 is unchanged. The additional experiments and video adaptation introduce no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same dataset, landmark-tokenization, geometry–appearance decoupling, identity-preservation, and performance claims. v2 explicitly names landmark-aware CFG in the abstract, but v1 already identifies and explains it as a contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting robustness to tokenization, fusion, and unconditional tokens, and attributes the largest codebook's weaker performance to instability and underutilization. It also states specific limits: identity degradation with severe landmark loss or occlusion, expensive on-the-fly processing, and a video extension that still requires driving videos. These qualify and extend the retained interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 documents the video adaptation's backbone, temporal length, annotation types, and frozen/trainable components. It supplies the human-study questionnaire with rating anchors and suggested viewing time, plus landmark rendering instructions for PSNR evaluation. Original implementation settings and the promise to release code and data upon acceptance remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gender Shades (Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018) to support demographic characterization and Wan (2025) for the video backbone. The related-work sections and positioning against existing face-editing approaches otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized abstract and caption revisions, additional experimental and appendix subsections, acknowledgements, and a dedicated limitations section. The publication header changes, but the main narrative and most existing prose remain intact rather than undergoing extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with challenging-input panels, ambiguous-instruction examples, video-animation sequences, and two new quantitative tables (Figures 6, 7, 11; Tables 8–9). Figure 4 is redrawn to expose positional mapping and conditional/unconditional pathways. Existing displays are retained and reflowed, including v1 Figure 6 becoming v2 Figure 8.

improvement.justification: The direct human-rating study strengthens validation beyond v1's automatic scores and identity-metric study, while the quantization ablation tests a central design choice. Explicit failure conditions improve the paper's account of applicability. These are useful gains, although robustness and video evidence remain primarily qualitative and the new quantitative results lack uncertainty reporting. The additions support a limited overall quality improvement.
